content: But in giving you this command I don’t praise you, because you come together not for the better but for the worse. {{v:18}} For first of all, when you come together in the assembly, I hear that divisions exist among you, and I partly believe it. {{v:19}} For there also must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be revealed among you. {{v:20}} When therefore you assemble yourselves together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. {{v:21}} For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken. {{v:22}} What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly and put them to shame who don’t have enough? What shall I tell you? Shall I praise you? In this I don’t praise you. {{v:23}} For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread. {{v:24}} When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.” {{v:25}} In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.” {{v:26}} For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. {{v:27}} Therefore whoever eats this bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way unworthy of the Lord will be guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord. {{v:28}} But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of the bread and drink of the cup. {{v:29}} For he who eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment to himself if he doesn’t discern the Lord’s body. {{v:30}} For this cause many among you are weak and sickly, and not a few sleep. {{v:31}} For if we discerned ourselves, we wouldn’t be judged. {{v:32}} But when we are judged, we are disciplined by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with the world. {{v:33}} Therefore, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. {{v:34}} But if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, lest your coming together be for judgment. The rest I will set in order whenever I come.

facets.text: Paul rebukes the Corinthians because their Eucharistic gatherings have become occasions of division rather than communion, with the wealthy eating their fill while the poor go hungry and are shamed. Such selfishness contradicts the very nature of the Lord's Supper, which is meant to unite the body of Christ. When charity toward the poorest member is despised, Paul declares that what they eat is no longer truly the Lord's Supper at all.
facets.question: How can social divisions and neglect of the poor corrupt the celebration of the Eucharist?

facets.text: Paul transmits the words of institution as sacred tradition he 'received from the Lord' and 'delivered' to the Church, using the technical language of authoritative handing-on. This makes 1 Corinthians the earliest written record of the Eucharistic words, predating the Gospels, and grounds the Mass in Christ's own command on the night he was betrayed. The faithful transmission of this tradition safeguards the identity of the sacrament across generations.
facets.question: Where does the Church's celebration of the Eucharist come from and how was it handed down?

facets.text: Over the bread Christ says 'This is my body' and over the cup 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood,' identifying the elements with his own self given up in sacrifice. The Catholic tradition reads these words as establishing the Real Presence and the new covenant sealed not in the blood of animals but in Christ's own blood. The Eucharist thus fulfills and surpasses the covenant sacrifices of the Old Testament.
facets.question: What do Christ's words 'this is my body' and 'the new covenant in my blood' mean about his presence in the Eucharist?

facets.text: Christ commands 'Do this in memory of me,' establishing the Eucharist as an ongoing memorial that is far more than a mental recollection. In the biblical sense of remembrance, the memorial re-presents and makes present the saving reality it commemorates. Thus every celebration of the Mass is the Church obeying this dominical command and entering into the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ.
facets.question: What does it mean that the Eucharist is celebrated as a memorial 'in memory of' Christ?

facets.text: Paul teaches that 'as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes,' giving the Eucharist a threefold temporal reach. It looks back to Calvary, is celebrated in the present as proclamation, and looks forward in hope to Christ's return. The Eucharist is therefore both a memorial of the passion and an anticipation of the parousia.
facets.question: How does the Eucharist connect Christ's past death, the present Church, and his future coming?

facets.text: Paul warns that receiving the body and blood 'in an unworthy way' makes one 'guilty of the body and the blood of the Lord' and brings judgment rather than grace. This presupposes that Christ is truly present, for one cannot be guilty of profaning a mere symbol. The command that a person 'examine himself' grounds the Catholic discipline of self-examination and repentance before receiving Communion.
facets.question: What does it mean to receive Communion unworthily and why is self-examination required beforehand?

facets.text: Failing to 'discern the Lord's body' is linked by Paul to weakness, sickness, and death among the Corinthians, which he interprets as the Lord's fatherly discipline rather than final condemnation. This chastisement is medicinal, meant to correct the community 'that we may not be condemned with the world.' Divine discipline in this life is thus a mercy that spares the faithful from ultimate judgment.
facets.question: Why does Paul connect misuse of the Eucharist with suffering, and how is divine discipline an act of mercy?

facets.text: Paul's practical remedy, to 'wait for one another' and to eat at home if merely hungry, restores the Eucharistic assembly to its proper purpose as a common act of the whole body. The gathering is not a private meal but the corporate worship of the Church, where mutual charity and reverence must govern conduct. Right liturgical order and love for one another are inseparable from authentic Eucharistic celebration.
facets.question: What does Paul teach about the communal charity and order that should govern Eucharistic worship?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Paul corrects abuses at the Corinthian Eucharist and hands on Christ's words of institution, teaching the Real Presence, the new covenant, the memorial and proclamation of the Lord's death, and the need for worthy reception, self-examination, and communal charity.

[MORAL | explicit]: Selfish divisions where the rich eat while the poor are shamed corrupt the gathering so it is no longer truly the Lord's Supper.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: Paul received and delivered the words of institution as sacred tradition, the earliest written Eucharistic account, grounding the Mass in Christ's command.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: 'This is my body' and 'the new covenant in my blood' establish the Real Presence and the covenant sealed in Christ's own blood, fulfilling Old Testament sacrifice.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: 'Do this in memory of me' institutes the Eucharist as a biblical memorial that re-presents Christ's saving sacrifice, not mere recollection.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The Eucharist proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, reaching back to Calvary, present as proclamation, and forward to the parousia.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Receiving unworthily makes one guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, presupposing Real Presence and requiring self-examination before Communion.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: Weakness, sickness, and death are read as the Lord's medicinal discipline meant to spare the faithful from condemnation with the world.
[MORAL | explicit]: Paul's remedy to wait for one another restores the assembly as corporate worship governed by charity and reverent order.
